utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon to everybody. Mr. Registrar would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon Your Honours. Good afternoon to everyone in the courtroom. This is case number IT-06-90-T, The Prosecutor versus Ante Gotovina et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Before we continue with the examination of Mr. Konings, I'd like to deal quickly with a few procedural matters. The Chamber was informed that there are no objections against admission of P1269 and P1270.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Therefore, P1269 and P1270 are admitted into evidence. Then, Mr. Russo, the Prosecution is invited -- because you're calling the witnesses and you may know best where there would be any time available, to find after the conclusion of the evidence of Mr. Konings to find in the next week for a housekeeping session and inform the Chamber and, of course, then the Defence as well what would be your preference. Then the Chamber is informed that there is some, although very limited agreement, on the coordinates or the coordination -- coordinate system used in some of the documents presented. If there's anything to report to the Chamber in this respect, we'd like to hear from you, Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes Mr. President. Unfortunately, what we have agreed on is that, I think, certainly I've had a conversation with Mr. Russo, and we have misunderstood what Mr. Russo indicated in court yesterday. It was your understanding that in fact the Office of the Prosecutor had taken these coordinates and plotted them out to see where they actually are. It turns out that in terms of actually plotting them out, the Prosecution has not done that. We have done that, and so there really was no point in sitting down and talking about whether we agree that these are the coordinates; and we intend to go through that in cross-examination of this witness as to where those coordinates are. And so we have agreed that at this point we can't have a meaningful conversation until the Prosecution, and I understand from Mr. Russo they will be in fact on their own, plotting the coordinates to see where they fall. But until time, Mr. Russo has indicated they will look what we put in, in cross-examination and unless this is an reason that they think the coordinate is not accurate, in which case they will object we'll proceed --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Of course, there are two distinct elements in this question. The first is what system of coordinates is used - is this the usual grid references - so the system that's one; and the second is that when plotting the coordinates on a map where we'll find ourselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: This is a -- not the usual system that the UN would use. This is it a separate system. It's Croatia zone 5 projection transverse. Merkator, I'm going to mispronounce this but Gauss-Kruger, G-a-u-s-s, hyphen Kruger, K-r-u-g-e-r; and the specifically Ellipsoid Bessel 1841 is the system.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Sounds grade.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: For the record what's what we're going to be using. JUGE ORIE: That's what you're going to be using, and Mr. Russo is informed about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, if I could also add that this is the system that the Yugoslav army, a coordinate system which they had in place, which is the basis upon which the Croatian army then used those coordinates --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I take if you have sufficient examples and it's not just the hospitals that you have verify in an experimental basis on whether, for example, if you have a reference to cross-roads whereas in plotting you signed yourself in the middle of a swimming pool then of course that might be a problem. So testing will certainly assist in finding the right understanding of the system that. That was the --

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Your Honour, my apologies. I just want to add something to what Mr. Misetic said. First of all, he is correct. I agree with everything he said. The -- we didn't actually speak about the coordinate system, in particular system he has identified. Nevertheless, I certainly take him at his word that this was the system used by the Croatian army. What I had indicated yesterday was -- which I think is in line with this, we had taken the Croatian maps which received from the government of Croatia upon your request, used those lines actually on the physical map to determine the box where the coordinates fell; so I would assume that those lines on the map correspond to the system he's mentioned, and I haven't seen the map that we're planning on showing the witness on cross-examination but again since they've already gone through the trouble of plotting it, we'll take a look at that once we've had it done on our computer system, I'm sure we'll come to some agreement on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. May I then take it that part of the motions yesterday arose from you -- well, arose on the basis of the understanding that you had plotted that already that some of the motion has went down in intensity.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: In intensity, yes. Then I also understand that there's no agreement on the word and I might also pronounce it wrongly, but stacionar whether that has intrinsic medical connotation as I do understand is suggested by the Prosecution on the basis of a dictionary or whether stacionar also exists without this connotation.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: If I could address, first on this. Your Honour, the reason that the dictionary page was provided was not an attempt by the Prosecution to end the issue of how exactly one defines the term stacionar. I understand from Mr. Misetic that this has a certain specific meaning in the military context. However, we were responding to the objection which was made yesterday by Mr. Kuzmanovic that the word stacionar could only mean one thing, and this is an explanation for why apparently whomever translated this at CLSS provided the word medical station in response to the word stacionar. So that is where the disagreement arises from, it's not a resolution of the issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do understand, well how to resolve it, of course there are two ways, either you further consult your linguistic experts --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I was just about to add, Mr. President, that Mr. Russo and I are in agreement that we should take some time, additional time to try to come to a common agreement as to what that word means in this context if we can; and if we can't one way or the other to report back to the Chamber on what we discussed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you for that information. Now, finally I was informed that some observations were to be made about the 1993 map that was shown to the Court yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour, and of course the previous issue of the word stacionar would be entirely mooted if the Court decided that the relevance of the document or were not probative enough for admission that that would obviate the previous issue. So probably first best to address the Defence's argument about whether or not assuming that in the word medical station is, in fact, medical station that the document is admissible.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, we object on relevance grounds and we object in terms of lack of probative value. Mr. Russo and I have had an additional discussions to see if in fact the 1993 Poskok map which was for the purposes of a training exercise was then subsequently used in Operation Storm in 1995. I think we're in agreement that there is no explicit reference to the fact that that map was used in Operation Storm. It is it our position that in fact it wasn't used in Operation Storm. There is no evidence to support such an assertion and therefore I know Mr. Russo will have -- will ask the Court to draw inferences because I think some of the targets may overlap in terms of what ultimately in other documents that were used in Operation Storm are similar - although not the stacionar issue - similar to some that are in the Poskok 93 map. I don't think that it's unusual that fixed targets would have remained the same in 1993 and in 1995. I don't think that means that the entire Poskok 93 map then should be taken as a map which was used in Operation Storm, A, or that all the targets in Poskok 93 were used in Operation Storm simply because some targets might overlap.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But now you're mixing up two things; first is whether it has any relevance at all or whether what conclusions to drawn from that. A map can be relevant even if you would not accept that all the targets for training purposes put on that map actually were used and that it depends on the totality of the evidence, whether any such conclusion would be justified or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I think, Your Honour, there would have to be more foundation to establish that this particular map was used. Some reference in a diary, some reference in a document an order saying to use that list and there -- as far as I know there is no such corroborative evidence to support that conclusion. Secondly, and this goes to the, quite frankly, to the fact of the prejudice outweighing the probative value. For to us admit this map would require the Defence then to start putting in evidence about what the circumstances were with respect to certain facilities on a 1993 map; and I will provide a good faith proffer to you that 1993 was different because there were troops of Arkan's Tigers, Captain Dragan's forces which weren't there in 1995. But we would have to go through that entire exercise of presenting evidence to the Chamber about targets in an exercise map from 1993 and the circumstances around why targets would be selected in that circumstance and to put things in the proper context, and I don't think that exercise really is a useful use of either the Defence's resources or quite frankly in terms of the overall scheme of things that the Trial Chamber needs to be inundated about targets in 1993 and what they were used for. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, whether that would be a logical consequence of a decision to admit is -- is still to be considered. But we'll further consider the matter. But the first question is if we would now already decide that the map would not be admitted under whatever circumstances then the issue of the stacionar would be moot. That's clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: On the basis of the submissions and the information the Chamber has received until now, it finds no reason to decide not to admit the map, which, of course, is not a final decision on admission; and we heard a lot of information such as it was for training purposes, it is from 1993, that's, of course, all information to the extent the parties agree on certain information; for example, that it is a 1993 map. If it appears somewhere on the map then, of course, it is easy for the Chamber to follow. But to the extent the parties agree on factual background of the map, the Chamber would invite the parties to present that to the Chamber, and we'll further look at this material to come to a final decision on admission, yes or no.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Does that mean that we'll receive a MFI and resolve the issue during the housekeeping session?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, during the housekeeping session or it depends on how matters develop. Whether the parties will be invited to make further decisions -- further submissions or do the parties -- well invited to provide further information on the map. It's difficult for me and for the Chamber having looked at this map only very briefly just being able to identify where we find the boxes with targets with unclear language at this moment to say anything more about it. Then I'd like to read a request for information the Chamber addresses to the parties, and that's the last procedural item I have on my agenda before we would proceed. It is a request for information from the parties regarding the scheduling of the remainder of the Prosecution case and the beginning of the Defence case. While the Chamber is well aware that there are a number of pending issues that may make it difficult to make an accurate prediction for the near future, the Chamber, nonetheless, views it as important that some sort of time-frame be set out as to give all parties an idea of what to expect. The Chamber, therefore, invites the Prosecution and each Defence team to make brief oral submissions on the following five questions, and the oral submissions will be heard on Friday, the 23rd of January of this year. Firstly, the Prosecution is asked to inform the Chamber on who the remaining Prosecution witnesses are, and on what date it expects to close its case. Secondly, the Defence teams are asked to inform the Chamber if they are intending to make submissions pursuant to Rule 98 bis of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence; and if so, how much time they would require for this. Thirdly, the parties are asked to inform the Chamber on how many working days they would ideally require between the last day of the Prosecution's case and a possible hearing for Rule 98 bis submissions. Fourthly, the Defence teams are asked to inform the Chamber on how many working days they would ideally require between a possible hearing for Rule 98 bis submissions and the start of the Defence case, if there is an need to present one. Fifthly, and finally, the Defence teams are asked to inform the Chamber, provided that there is an need to present a case, in which order they would like to present their evidence. In its planning, the Chamber will do its utmost to take the parties' wishes into account. And this concludes the Chamber's request for information. If there are no other procedural matters at this moment --

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Your Honour, my apologies, we need a MFI number for the Poskok map. That's 65 ter 6128.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I thought we would do that when we resumed but there is no problem in assigning a MFI number to the map. Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that becomes Exhibit P1273, marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Mr. Usher, could you please escort Mr. Konings into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Konings.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we continue, I'd like to remind you that the solemn declaration you gave at the beginning of your testimony is still binding you. I also noticed that you brought some material with you. It's no problem whatsoever, but if you want to consult any material that was not provided to you by the usher, I'd like you to first address me and indicate that you wish to consult that material and what it is. Mr. Russo.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Colonel Konings. I'd like to begin today by taking a look at a map of the planned activities of the 4th Guards Brigade which, as you point out in your addendum, was one of the professional brigades tasked with taking the town of Knin.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, if we could please have 65 ter 5037.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Now, Colonel, once the map comes up on the screen, you may recall that this is one of the maps shown to you by the OTP and that it's rather large map, difficult to see in any detail. I'd like to show it to you first and ask if you recall seeing this map?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have seen this map before.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And I'd like to concentrate first on the text which appears on the map.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And, Your Honour, we have translated the text on the map. I'll ask Mr. Registrar to pull up, please, the translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And you can see at the beginning here is the information of who the map was approved by, who it is signed by, what the title of the map is; and then if we can proceed a bit lower, it indicates the table of contents which corresponds to the legend which appears on the map. And you'll note that the second line in the table of contents indicates self-propelled multiple rocket launcher fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: If we could now have 65 ter 6446.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Now, Colonel Konings, for your information and for the Chamber's information as well, what we have done is enlarged sections of the map that I'd like to show. We have enlarged in particular the table of contents and the portion of the map around Knin that I'd like to focus on.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: If we could perhaps spin the map portion.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: You'll also notice there the table the contents and as I read before the second line indicating multiple-barrel rocket launcher fire and you'll see that that corresponds to a green target box on the left hand of your screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Now if we can move to the second page of the map itself, and I don't believe we need the translation from this point further. If we could just move to the second page of this exhibit. If we could enlarge the area around the two green -- there we are.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: You'll see, Colonel Konings, that two of the green target boxes appear in Knin in two different areas, and I'll simply -- before I move on to the next page in this exhibit, I'll ask to you take note of the fact that at the -- looking at the bottom green square, you'll see the image which comes up along the right-hand side of that green target box and which the green target box partly covers and goes through corresponds to the railway tracks in the town of Knin. And what appears immediately to the left of the green target box which is outlined in black immediately to the left of the bottom green target box corresponds to the Knin fortress, and that is just to give you an idea of the relative location of the box itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: So if we could move to the next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: What we've done here, Colonel Konings, is superimposed the location of those squares or approximate location of those squares over the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: If we could just move down.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And here again you'll notice the railroad tacks coming up on the right-hand side and into the bottom box which on this particular page is blue and that the outline to the immediately left of the bottom blue square represents the Knin fortress.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And if we could again move to the next and final page of this exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: What we have attempted to do here, and if we could just spin that again, please. What we have attempt to do here is superimpose the approximate locations of those boxes on the aerial photograph which we're all familiar by now. I can tell that you and inform the Chamber that the slight warping of those boxes is due to the angle at which this photograph was taken - at least that's what I'm told - that the GO referencing software which was used to superimpose these boxes resulted in a slight skewing based on the angle of which the photograph was taken. So looking at this area, I'd like to ask you a few questions about the use of multiple-barrel rocket launchers in civilian-populated areas. In section 10 of your expert report, you indicated that generally that rockets are less accurate than Howitzers. And what I'd like to you do is please comment for the Chamber on whether you believe it is appropriate to use multiple-barrel rocket launchers to fire at any targets in a civilian-populated area.

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I have to come back to the points that we already discussed the days before. Firing in a civilian-populated area with any weapon system, with any indirect firing weapon systems, is dependant on many factors and we have been debating: The value of a military target in a civilian area, the proximity of the civilian elements in that area which are the most important and, of course, the accuracy or inaccuracy of the weapon systems that you have available. There are three important factors that may take -- that may a commander bring to the decision to use indirect fire weapon systems. But at the lower end of indirect fire systems there where you talk about inaccuracy are the regular rocket systems. As long as they are not guided missiles, they suffer from more inaccuracy than the artillery or -- than Howitzer or mortar systems. That has to be -- that is caused by the fact that a rocket mortar burns through a certain period of time and the controllable -- to control that exact burning time well, there is a difference between each rocket. So once you are able to have exactly the same burning time in combination with a guided system inside a rocket then have you an accurate rocket, and I can refer to various guided missile systems in use all over the world where you are able to pinpoint a rocket through a window of a house. But as far as my knowledge reaches these rocket launchers in use nor rocket launchers in use in other countries in the world at that time, they used regular unguided rocket systems, which brings me to the conclusion that they have a larger inaccuracy than a regular artillery projectile. So using those rockets inside a quite large area with a lot of civilian elements in there would not be my choice in order to attack a military -- a small, relative small target in that area. Rockets are extremely area weapon systems. They are not fit to do point -- point targets unless what I said before they have the capacity of GPS on board or any other guided missile system.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Your Honour, think would move for the admission of 65 ter 5037 and 65 ter 6446.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] ... sorry, the 65 ter 5037 is the large map. 65 ter 6546 is the smaller, I take it of that. The issue that I have is on the map that was superimposed. If we can go back one map in this list. If you can spin that for me, please. You can see, Judge, that the top square is not accurate vis-a-vis 65 ter 6446. That top square should be further over to the left. So to the extent that the Prosecution can make that more accurate, we can take a look at it at that point. With regard to 65 ter 5037 and 65 ter 6446, we have no objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You said the -- let me just ... Top square, the top of the two in the original green, here kind of a blue purple you said it should be more to the --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Left.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Left.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: To the left. If we go back to 65 ter 6446. We can see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: This is 6446. I think you want the aerial photograph it's the next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: That's fine. What I'm dealing is the larger map where we then focussed in on the squares in Knin.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: That would be the first page of this particular exhibit. If you're looking for the original map portion that is covered by the boxes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let us look then at the first page of this document and compare it to this. I think Your Honours will see what I'm talking about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: This one is inaccurate. What we see on our screen now, Mr. Kehoe. Is that --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: That's correct, Judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. What I see on this map is that the left limit, the left border of the upper square is in a south/north direction almost exactly at the same position as the -- what appears to be the fortress. Now looking at the original map, that seems to be -- well, I'm not saying by the millimetre but approximately the case in the -- in the original as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: If I could add, Your Honour, the feature that we used I think is the reference point. If you look to the -- the right-hand side of the top square, you'll see that the -- it covers the railroad crossing where the railway bridge goes over the railroad tracks; and that's where you will see on the original you follow the railroad tracks from the top of the bottom green box to the bottom of the top green box you will see that it also crossed over the railway bridge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If there are differences, they are very limited. Would you agree with that Mr. Kehoe?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I agree that they're limited, Judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll see to what extent the details in the precision here is important. If it turns out to be important, then I would say that Mr. Russo will be invited to do his homework, but let's not deal with tens of millimetres at this moment if we are not knowing yet what the importance of it is it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes? Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter 5037 becomes Exhibit P1274; and 65 ter 6446 becomes Exhibit P1275.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: My apologies, Your Honour, I don't know if it would be more beneficial to the Court to have both of these collapsed into one exhibit since it might be more useful unless the Court thinks that there's a chance that the second enlargement won't be as useful in interpreting a larger map. In any case, it is just a suggestion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, I'm relatively neutral on the matter. Of course, we will focus on what is the source material. That is most important. But I do -- now, again reference to the numbers, 5037 was the --

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: That's the original map, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's the original map. And 6446 is the series of two projections is that ...

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. P1274 and P1275 are admitted into evidence, with the proviso that, if the projections will need further precision, that this can be decided on an application, once it has become clear what the importance of these details is. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. If we could now have 65 ter 5742.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Now, Colonel Konings, what we have just looked at was a map which was a plan of action for the 4th Guards Brigade which of course you do address in your expert report. The document we're looking at now is an artillery expenditure report of the 4th and 7th Guards Brigade for the 4th and 5th of August, and you will notice on the fourth row where it indicates that 248 multiple-barrel rocket launchers were fired on those dates. And in conjunction with the testimony you gave to my last question, if even a small number of these 248 rockets were fired into Knin, do you think, in your opinion, is that appropriate use of artillery in a civilian-populated area?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as I told before, the inaccuracy of a rocket system is larger so they are less accurate than an artillery round; and I do think I have expressed my opinion that an artillery round -- the use of artillery in a civilian-populated area is not the best or most logical choice to use unless you have a military target in a civilian-populated area that is outside the -- the collateral damage rate. I gave you an example yesterday about those 500 metres that we used in Afghanistan. And I have to come back to the fact that you have to estimate every time over and over again the value of the military target that you want to combat, the proximity of the civilian population, and the effectiveness of your projectiles that you use. And I can only repeat that unguided rocket projectiles come at the end of the scale, at the lower end of the scale. So given me the information that the military targets in Knin were of very low value for the defence of Knin, my choice would not have been using rockets against any targets in the areas inside Knin especially not in those areas that you showed me before. Because in those areas we saw yesterday, there were military targets located; but they were all confined in a civilian-populated area with close proximity of civilian buildings with the large -- with the possibility that civilians are still in that buildings so my choice, if I would have seen the need of taking out military targets in such a confined civilian-populated area, my choice would not be not to use this rocket systems.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Now if a commander decided to use artillery against a particular target in Knin; for example, against the ARSK headquarters, in your opinion what other considerations or -- let me ask that in another way. In your opinion, what would be the reason, military reason or what military advantage would be gained by using a rocket as opposed to, for example, a 130-millimetre gun?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is -- I'm sorry I have to come back to the aspects that I tried to explain already before, is it is, first of all, a matter of importance of the target, and if an ARSK headquarter may be qualified as an important target in itself. But as we discussed before, that headquarters is in a strong building, so the use of artillery is not the most -- is not the choice to make because it is sheer impossible to destroy such a building in a way that you can take out the headquarters, if the headquarters is already there. But let's assume that the headquarters is up and running in such a building. It is very hard to take out that complete headquarters with the use of artillery. Given the inaccuracy of rocket projectiles, the chance of hitting that headquarters is less. The chance of hitting the environment is -- the -- the -- the arrows that you have in length and width, especially in length, from a rocket are bigger than artillery; so you have more chance of projectiles that fall short of the building or fall plus of the building. So given that inaccuracy I would not choice rockets. If the ARSK headquarters is a high pay-off target, and I can imagine that it is when it is occupied and when it is up and running, then the -- the choice would be taking a more accurate weapon system which in this case is artillery but then comes in that you have the chance that you will have collateral damage in a civilian environment; but I cannot stress enough that is up to the commander on the scene given his rules of engagement to decide whether he takes that headquarters out with artillery, yes or no.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And can you give the Chamber some idea of what kind of damage could be done to the ARSK HQ since you mentioned the construction of the building itself. What would rockets do to a building like that?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, a rocket filled with a high explosive charge will probably have the same, more or less, the same influence on a building as a high explosive of a -- as a high explosive round of a 155 or 152. Those rockets are also area weapon systems especially effective against unarmoured personnel, against personnel in the open, against lightly armoured vehicles so they will -- if they hit the building, they will cause damage. That's for sure. They will make holes they will maybe even destroy a roof. But the damage will be comparable with what I described on artillery rounds.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you. Your Honour, at this time, I would move for admission of 65 ter 5742.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: No objection, Judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P1276, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is admitted into evidence. Mr. Konings, could you remind me, the TF shells, TF rockets that stands for time --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Time fuse.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Time fuse. So there is a timing when they will explode.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They will probably explode probably in the form of an air bust, and produce shrapnel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, although time, of course, is a variable which means that just on the basis of TF shell or TF rocket you can't identify whether it will be an air burst or a burst upon -- after impact.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well no you -- you -- that in itself doesn't say anything because a time fuse, when it is not timed, when it is not -- when the time is not set will explode as a normal point detonating fuse.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Upon impact.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Upon impact, yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And just to follow up on His Honour Judge Orie's question, with a time fuse is there ever a reason to set the timer to explode after the point of impact? In other words, if you wanted the shell to explode before it actually impacts in order to create a time fuse, is that what -- in order create an air burst my apologies. Is that what a time fuse is for, or is there any other reason for a time fuse?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not quite sure I understand the question correct, Mr. Russo. Could you please rephrase it.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Sure. You said that a time fuse a projectile, with a time fuse on it, if the time fuse is not set, the projectile once it impacts will simply impact and explode like a regular point detonating projectile. So what is the purpose of having a timer on the fuse if not to explode before it impacts?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that can be -- I don't know. That can be many reason. There can be lack of point detonating fuses in stock. There are various reasons to think about. Normally the artillery rounds in stock can be provided with either point detonating or time fuses. I'm not quite sure how that works with the rocket systems. The rocket systems that we have in the Netherlands are equipped with a variable fuse that is standard on the rocket, so you cannot change that yourself. But artillery rounds, you screw the fuse on top of that before you fire it. If you have a point detonating fuse variable and you want to act in a point detonating mode, then you will not screw a time fuse in there because you may them in a limited number available. So a commander, a battery commander, or an artillery commander would only order time fuses to use time fuse, if you want to accurately use air burst. That again can be decisions on the spot. You might be short of point detonating fuses, you might be ordered to deliver a fire for a fact, and then can you use time fuses that are operating as a point detonating fuse. But it is a more expensive way of doing because a time fuse is more expensive than a point detonating fuse, but maybe on this time in operation nobody cares about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I ask one further question because I also had some difficulties in finding out for myself what your problem was. Is it true that there are also fuses which have a kind of delayed detonation so upon impact that it will take another quarter of a second to detonate, so that first the projectile can enter the construction and then explode once it is -- it may have entered through a roof or whatever. Now, would you call that also a time fuse or does that have a different name so as when we read here time fuse shell that it's not a reference to such a kind of delayed detonation device.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The -- a delayed function is a function that is an extra function on a point detonating fuse and has nothing to do with a time fuse, so it ask just a matter of turning a small screw inside, inside the fuse, you can do that just before you fire the projectile which gives the function a short delay so that you have the effect that you -- that you already described, a projectile will explode a split second later than when hitting the ground or to enter the building and will explode then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, TF would not be any reference for you to such a kind of detonation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no, no, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I also have now a document that I would like to move across the bar table, this being 65 ter 5957. This was on the exhibit list for Colonel Konings. However, it simply demonstrates use of MBRLs fired on Knin on the 4th of August by a different operational group, so I don't see the need to show it to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, just the same request if we just MFI it, and I can take a look at and just report back quickly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours that becomes Exhibit P1277, marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And it will keep that status for the time being. Please proceed, Mr. Russo.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you. If we could please have Exhibit P64.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Now, Colonel Konings, I'm going to show you a document which was prepared by the senior UNMO in Knin approximately two weeks after the artillery attack and ask you for your comments on the document. Now, first have you had a chance to review this document prior to coming to court today?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have -- I have had the opportunity to study this document, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And I'd like to focus in particular on paragraph 2 and ask you --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Excuse me, counsel if I have the reference in the report where he discusses this.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: There's no reference in the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: There's no reference in the report. My understanding, Judge, is if we were talking for expert opinion on particular issues that has to be somewhat reflected in a report. I was interested to note during the preparation of both reports that some months and months and months apart that this document had not been discussed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could we first ask: When did you see this document, Mr. Konings.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the preparation of -- together with the OTP. The OTP has showed me this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: A couple of days ago.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: A long time ago.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Several times in our preparation phase and that preparation phase runs already well, more than a year.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Russo, have you invited Mr. Konings to comment on this.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Your Honour, Colonel Konings' comments on this are included in the supplemental information sheet. The proofing note which came out of the proofing section between 26th and 28th of November.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We haven't seen the proofing notes. Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: It's an interesting -- I notice -- a proofing note. This is a document that obviously has been or was received from the Prosecution and obviously has been central of this case going back to, I think, to March. It was not disclosed in his -- various reports. The last of which I note was filed by the Office of the Prosecutor on the 30th of October, 2008. It looks as if we are getting yet another undisclosed expert opinion, and I don't think that putting it in a supplemental information sheet suffices. Certainly not under Rule 94 bis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber will allow Mr. Russo to put this question to the witness. If it causes any further need for the preparation of cross-examination, the Chamber would like to know. The Chamber does not exclude for the possibility that this report, this specific report, that the specific relevance of it rather than to be part of the report in its entirety came up at a later stage. Mr. Russo you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Colonel Konings, I would like to focus -- or I would like you to focus on paragraph 2 and tell the Chamber whether the information which is reported here, assuming, of course, that it's accurate, whether that information would change the opinions you have expressed in your addendum regarding the artillery attack on Knin.

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it describes the fact that the conclusion of the UNMOs was that shelling was, in general, concentrated against military objectives. We have discussed various military objectives throughout the city and that another conclusion is that the damage caused by shelling to civilian establishments is concentrate to the close vicinity of military objectives. That seems to be logic to what I have tried to explain is that once you start shelling inside a close confined civilian area, small military targets, rather small military targets that this is what happens that rounds not only on military target but in the civilian area around it. And that says that the use of artillery in such an area may not be the best choice to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, moving to paragraph 3 where it indicates that a block of flats is count the as one figure. And further down it indicates that 21 buildings were found to have been severely damaged by shelling and an additional 23 buildings were found to have been slightly damaged by shelling. Can you tell the Chamber whether this amount of damage changes your opinion that you have expressed about whether the artillery attack should have taken place on the 4th of August?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If I may, Judge, with all due respect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: This is a question that should have been asked to a witness that the Prosecution took off the witness list, Lieutenant-Colonel Hjertnes, who could explain what he observed and what his UNMOs observed in this. We are talking about a question that is completely in the abstract without any frame of reference and fairness to the witness to what exactly Lieutenant-Colonel Hjertnes is talking about when he is talking about these buildings. They could have asked the proper person the question. They chose not to. And the 23 buildings are those military buildings? Are they civilian buildings? It doesn't say that.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't know that it is necessary to get in these issues with the witness on the stand. But the Court will recall that we did call several of the UNMOs who actually conducted the survey, and again they said that Lieutenant-Colonel Hjertnes did not, himself, conduct the survey. They conducted it. They provide information about the fact that they couldn't get into any of the military installations and they didn't know which particular targets Lieutenant-Colonel Hjertnes was referring to in paragraph 2. All of that aside, I'm simply asking the witness to offer his opinion whether this level of damage, as it is clearly stated on the document whether it seems to change his opinion about whether the attack should have taken place and how appropriate it was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, first of all, this witness cannot testify about the accuracy of the observations in this report. The Chamber does not fully understand your objection because the opinion of the witness is as it is now. Mr. Russo invites him to see whether this changes his opinion. Well, there are two possible answers. One is yes. And, of course, we wouldn't know whether that would be in favour of the Defence, but it tends at least, I understand the question to be, would this mean that -- well, that the opinion of the witness about the appropriateness of using this weapon system would change and in view of the opinion he expressed on the matter it -- I would say I would expect it to be more favourable to the Defence. The other answer is that it doesn't change anything and matters are as they are. Although we do not fully understand the purpose but in view of the extent to which the question and the answer to it, at this moment, assists the Chamber, we will not ask the witness to answer the question. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Do you need me to repeat the question, Colonel Konings?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. Well, the witness is not invited to answer the question then there is no need to repeat the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: My apologies, I misread. In that case, Your Honour, I have a video to show the witness it is quite lengthy, approximately it is between 15 and 20 minutes. I don't know if the Court would prefer a break and then play the video or --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Twenty minute would bring us to the break and would give an opportunity to Mr. Konings to consider what he has seen over the break and then also to ask whether there are any specific portions he would like to see again. So I think it would be the right thing to do is to play it, then have a break, and then we put the questions to Mr. Konings.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. We'll be playing a clip from 65 ter 3759 and we'll play it via Sanction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. There is one other matter. Questions to be put after a 20 minutes' footage might ask again for looking again at certain details. Do you have a list somewhere that you can easily find.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: I'm not going to be asking about particular portions but in general and for the Court's information I'm going to be asking the witness about what he hears on the video if he hears, what his interpretation is of the sounds of the artillery attack.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then nevertheless what he hears at that moment of the 20 minutes is still to be seen but let's look at the video and let's listen to the video.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President, could we just have a source of this video. Which video is this?

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: This is the Zastava film. Its's 65 ter 3759.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I believe th Zastava film uncut has been put into evidence to some degree, that's what i thought it was. There have been two versions of the Zastava film put into evidence. One that was an edited version by the Prosecution, one that was more fullsome that was admitted, I forget the name of the witness, but I believe it was a protected witness. Is it the same video that was here before or is this a different?

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: It's the same video. There are portions of the larger section which I took out where someone is walking through an apartment building and that kind of stuff. This is a shortened clip.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It is a selection of portions from the complete video from what I understand, which is in evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour. I can provide the time references. It's actually broken into two clips from 1 minute 45 seconds to 5 minutes 52 seconds of the Zastava film then it picks up again at 7 minutes 2 seconds and goes to 21 minutes 35 seconds.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Does that provide sufficient information Mr. Kehoe?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I believe the disclosure was on Zastava film. My question was whether or not it was something that was in evidence already that we were just re-repeating, if this is in fact a [Overlapping speakers] ... I'm still not clear on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, it's a new selection and perhaps it is very practical rather than to at a later stage to invite people to find specific portions to have it as a separate -- doesn't take any further paper or just electronic capacity. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Colonel Konings --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Russo, you said it was 4 minutes and 14 minutes, and which makes 18. I don't remember that I have seen 18 minutes of video footage until now.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: It could have been that the second clip was cut short, Your Honour; however, I think gotten --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: To avoid confusion, the times you gave are not the times as we see them on the videos because they have -- this is an new time starting at zero seconds. So actually you have not fully played what you said you would play. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: That's correct, Judge.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Colonel Konings, based on what you could hear of the shelling and specifically the rate of fire, are you able to offer the Chamber any insight into what kind of fire this is, if it is the destruction fire, neutralisation fire, or however any other kind of fire that you can describe?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour, I mean frankly that type of -- this particular piece of information from what we just say is just speculation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We do not know. Let's wait and see what the witness can tell us about -- apparently you're talking about frequency of the sounds heard, perhaps the type of sounds heard, I have no idea. But whether it will be speculation or it is still to be seen. And may I take it, Mr. Russo, that your' referring to the first portion of the video or to all of them because then we night need -- I had -- saw quite huge portions of the second part were almost without sound. So, therefore, could you please direct the witness to the portions you intended to refer to.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Specifically referring to the first portion of the video, the portion which was for the most part filmed in the dark. Can you offer the Chamber any insight specifically with respect to the rate of fire, what type of fire that is, in your opinion?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: You could notice different types of rates. First of all, you could note they were more in the background a higher rate of fire, several explosion short to each other, five, six, seven, something like that. That meet to a -- let's say a use of a fire for effect on a certain target. Of course, I do not know which target and exactly where it was in the environment. It was more on the background. And the other observation that I can make is that many rounds were fired as single rounds. So I couldn't hear any connection to a concentrate rate of fire that you expect to be fired according to the details that we saw in the target list where you see 50 rounds on a certain target in a short time-frame because otherwise the effect on the military target is gone if you [indiscernible] that time frame. So on one hand, I could observe a kind of fire for effect on a target, let's call -- let's assume a military target surrounded by numerous single rounds and many of them were artillery rounds because that's what I can recognise from the sound. And, unfortunately, I have recognised that in Sarajevo many times myself. That is the observations that I can give you, and those single rounds, it's hard for me to establish them to a -- to a certain target. I cannot do that. And if I have to classify those rounds, I would say they are interdiction. So making the life of people in the city including the military, well, chaotic not knowing where the next round will fall.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And can you tell the Chamber what effect on a military target firing single rounds at it will do as opposed to a fire for effect?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can assure you that every round will have its effect. No matter how trained you are, no matter how experienced you are, the use of artillery and mortar rounds in close proximity makes you think about what to do there and either to stay there, yes or no. But if you are in a protected area, in a building that can stand against those single rounds, trained soldiers probably will take the decision to stay and wait until the next things to happen. Untrained soldier, less trained soldiers, and civilians might be brought to chaos, to panic, to leave that location, to try to get to another location because if do you not know what the effects can be, if you do not have the idea what interdiction brings to you, then you might take the decision to leave that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Mr. President, I have no further questions for the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Russo. Then we'll first have a break. What will be the sequence after the break. Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You will be the first one. Perhaps we already ask the witness to leave the courtroom. We'd like to see you back after the break, a break of 25 minutes. And then I'd like to inquire with the parties on time estimates.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I have about three days of cross.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: We don't have any questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kuzmanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, depending on what Mr. Kehoe asks, half a day to a day for me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Half a day to a day. As always, the Chamber, in granting the time, and the Chamber, of course, is aware of the importance of this expert, this witness, we'll also -- as always, keep an eye on the -- how effective and how efficient the cross-examination is conducted. We will resume at ten minutes past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Konings, you will now be cross-examined by Mr. Kehoe. Mr. Kehoe is counsel for Mr. Gotovina. Please proceed, Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Colonel Konings. It's a pleasure to meet you, sir. Colonel, just a couple of questions, some background questions and then we'll try to dive into your report as quickly as possible.

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: With regard to -- just a couple of items on the preparation, maybe even something before that, with regard to your rank, sir, you have been a lieutenant-colonel since 1992; is that right?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: During that period of time, even before that, since you have been working with artillery have you had training in HV tactics and HV armaments, and how the HV or Croatian army operated?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not specifically training in HV tactics. We always have been trained in the past, before 1992, in the operations of the Warsaw Pact and after that, of course, we prepare ourselves in the specific operation that we are entering in.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Okay. And the Warsaw Pact, of course, was -- the JNA was not in the Warsaw Pact?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I do think that the way the JNA operated resembled quite a lot the way that the forces of the Warsaw Pact operated.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Okay, sir. I'm not going to through the items that are in your CV, sir. I would like to ask you a question though and it comes from the statement that you gave to the Office of the Prosecutor on 31st of May, 2006, in the Dragomir Milosevic case; and if we could just view this via Sanction. You see the first page, sir, and if we could just go to the second page in the second paragraph. In the first line of that paragraph 2 you note that: "I have had extensive experience with the technical, tactic, and operational use of artillery mortars and in particular and fire support in general. I would not characterise myself as an expert, rather, that I have a good knowledge of mortar and artillery systems, ammunitions, and their operational use." So I'm a little confused by this Colonel which is my I brought it to your attention about now characterising yourself as an expert in - I don't want to put words in your mouth, sir - these forms of artillery. Could you help us out here, sir, as to what you meant as not being an expert as opposed to just being an officer with good knowledge of mortar, and artillery systems, ammunition, and their operational use?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I think I can recall exactly what I was stating in that period. An expert to me that's extraordinary. I don't think that in our army there are experts running around. Maybe an expert in a very specific field of operation like we call it an ammunition expert. That's a guy or a woman who knows everything about a specific area. I rather prefer to call myself a person that knows a lot about a lot of issues; but I hate to call myself an expert because that's not -- I'm not a person to call myself an expert. People around me consider me to be an expert, including my current commanding officer, and including current -- previous commanding officers, in so far, they think I'm an expert, that they ask me to extend my retirement because I should have been retired two years ago and apparently they are very glad do have me and they ask me to extent my retirement up to 2011 when I'm 60 years old, so it's just my personality that I do not want to call myself an expert. It's just a personal thing, but I can assure you that persons around me call me an expert in, not only mortar and artillery, but in land operations in general.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Fair enough, sir. I hope they're paying you more money?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, they don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, sir, when I was looking at your report you noted that you had been given 60 documents prior to the preparation of your first report; is that right?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall the exact number whether it was 60 or 50, I have been given numerous document, yes, in preparation of my report.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And those documents were given to you by the OTP?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And I mean Mr. Russo specifically?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not only Mr. Russo. Also Mr. Tieger give me several of these reports and his whole team. So I have received reports under the responsibility I have all the considered either Mr. Russo or Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Prior to the preparation of your first report, did you review trial briefs in this case?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: What do you mean with trial briefs?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Legal documents that were filed by the Office of the Prosecutor and the Defence.

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I just concentrated myself on the reports -- on the information that was given to me by the OTP since they had specific questions about those aspects and I, of course, have been looking for information on the ICTY web site in trying to find, and I found, certain aspects of the case -- in general as they are on the Internet web site.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And what did you find out on the web site that you found out about the case? Can you help us out there?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was just interested in the people that are -- are here and the people that are be -- convicted from certain aspects that they -- that they were doing or not doing in -- in that period. So that I had a -- a clue in who I was -- who we were talking about and I did the same in my preparation for the General Dragomir Milosevic because they -- I don't know the people. I would be happy to meet them in person to have a lengthy chat with them, as professional soldiers between each other and to hear from them what their reason were to do the things as they apparently happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Sir, let me take a step further with what information you had in your possession. You received these series of documents that are listed in your report. Did you review any witness statements?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not review any witness statements.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Did you ask for any witness statements for clarification on certain points?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, if you would not mind, I'd like to clarify one issue which is a bit unclear in the transcript. I think I heard the witness say that people are being convicted, it says conflicted from certain aspects that they were doing or not doing. When you use the word convicted, did you want to say charged with, or convicted means, in legal terms it means that it has been established by a Court. That's not what you wanted --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was just trying to find the right word, so my apologies. I didn't mean the word convicted, I just wanted to say they are apparently charged with certain things that they have done or not have done in the past.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I would like to have that clear. Mr. Kehoe, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: You did review various military doctrinal manuals during the preparation of your report, be the UN manual -- excuse me, US, United States manual or NATO or manuals that were written by the Dutch army; is that right?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I, first of all, I specifically used a Dutch armour field manual or fire support; and secondly I used, of course, not only physical, but in the back of my mind, my knowledge of the rest of the Dutch army field manuals on doctrine on every type of operation. And besides that I, of course, have knowledge of NATO manuals NATO AJP's as we call them, NATO joint publications of various levels; and of course I have some knowledge of US army and UK army documents as well. But did I not specifically use them as a reference for my report.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And we will address ourselves during the questioning to some of the items in the manuals. Thank you for that clarification. I would like to ask you this question, Colonel, concerning your first report. Prior to the preparation of your first report, did you understand that the targeting in Knin by artillery was an issue of dispute in this case between the OTP and the Defence? Did you understand that?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In the preparation of the case, I can recall -- yes, I understood that -- that there was a dispute going on between both sides, and the fact that I was asked to be, to act as an expert for this court already proves that there is a kind of dispute going on about the use of artillery and mortars towards Knin.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: My question is a bit more focussed and my question relates to targeting.

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Did you know prior to your first report, Colonel, that there was an issue regarding targeting in Knin?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I tried to say in my former answer exactly the same where you are aiming at. The use of fire support means, includes to me everything. That includes also targeting, decision-making, use of [indiscernible] service, delivery means; so when I talk about fire support, I talk about the whole system and not about -- I cannot disconnect various elements from fire support because they're all connected, and fire support does not work when you take out one of the elements.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let's sharpen this question a little bit and you didn't discuss targeting issues -- the specific targeting issues in your first report, did you?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was talking about targeting in general but not on specific issues concerning Knin, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Is there some reason why in your first report you didn't discuss individual targets in Knin?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Why I did not do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Did not that?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is the approach that was followed by OTP. I was first, I can't recall exactly when that happened but on a certain moment in time, I have been approached by the OTP whether I was able to provide them as an expert the use of fire support, the application, the -- of fire support and that's where my first report was aiming at. It was specifically asked by OTP to write generic report about the -- all the ins and outs, all the aspects of fire support in general. So in that report, the OTP did not ask me to concentrate on targeting issues concerning Knin.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, was that first report written with the idea - and that idea coming from the OTP - that you would be asked to write yet another report dealing with targets in Knin?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: They told me this was a specific case concerning Knin but in their preparation they first needed that first report, and I think that they have built up it step by step in asking me to come up later on with a -- an extra report which concentrated on Knin, but I do think that was their approach; and I have just answered their questions in whatever they ask me to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And please don't misunderstand me. I realise that you were just following what you were requested to do. I don't want you to misunderstand my question. But I guess my last question on this is: When you were doing your first report, and you didn't discusses the targets that you put in your second report, when you were filing your first report was that being written with the understanding that you were going to file yet another one sometime down the line?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Because that was told by me -- that was told to me by the OTP that you knew the case where it was all about. But the way the OTP was operating is that they first needed a general understanding of what fire support in general does and cannot do, and that's the aim of the first report. And then later on, the OTP built from that report, they came with the focussed questions on the targeting issues in my addendum.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Who told you when you were doing your first report that you were going to be asked to do a second report detailing this targeting?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as far as I can recall because that is some one and a half year ago that that must have been Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If I may move to another subject, Colonel. And I would like to talk generally about some issues that you discussed during direct examination and certainly some questions that were asked by Judge Orie concerning the bases of your opinion and the framework for your opinion. And you have had training, sir, during the course of your career in the laws of armed conflict; have you not?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And you -- you all of a sudden -- not all of a sudden, that has been incorporated in your career, and you use at least portions of that during your training that you done during your career; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The laws are the basis for the -- in the Dutch state for the -- for the armed forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Okay. Now, just by -- before we move on, have you ever written any legal treatise or anything on the laws on armed conflict?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: When you were preparing your expert report, did you consult any academic or military legal journals in the preparation of that report?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I have been using the documents where I referred to, where it gives the explanation on legitimacy as far as I need to know, and I have had a short consultation with a colleague of mine who is a legal officer in the Dutch army.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, Colonel, you understand based on the training that you had that the laws on armed conflict are of a universal application and apply to conflicts throughout the world wherever they may be. You understand that?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I understand that armed --that the laws of armed conflict and also humanitarian laws as they are laid down in various agreements that they are applicable for every country, yes, everywhere in the world. Let's say, let's correct myself, they had should be applicable.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Exactly. That is the ideal, of course, that they should be. And as you move away from that, each individual country or NATO, the United States, they have their own military doctrine within each country and possibly even with NATO, don't they?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is, of course, every country has its own doctrine, and I only can confer to NATO. NATO has also common doctrine to which all countries -- which is up to the countries whether they ratify that, implement that, yes or no. That's the freedom that countries have inside NATO.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I would like to bring up 1D65-0127. Mr. President, if I can just digress for one second, not on the questioning, but these two documents that I'm going to be referring to 1D65-0172 and 1D65-0227, I will be flipping back and forth to them over the next various segments and at the risk of driving Mr. Monkhouse or the registry crazy it might be difficult time-wise to flip back and forth. So with the Chamber's permission, if I could give hard copies to the Chamber and the other side and, of course, the witness, it may be easier to move through this a bit more expeditiously with hard copy as opposed to waiting at every point for this to come up on the screen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that might be very practical although for the Chamber, of course, we can fix one of the documents in our own system and look at the other screen for the other one; so therefore with some inventivity [sic] we might resolve the problem but it is certainly appreciated that you are concerned about our well-being.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: It's just, I was talking and thinking about, Judge -- it's just this flipping back and forth, and putting it back and forth on the screen, the time-lag becomes difficult.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Colonel, this is the allied joint doctrine. Are you familiar with this document?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Okay. Just wait for my colleagues to -- all set? Okay. I'd like to turn to page 2 of 16. I believe that maybe the next page on this, if I have uploaded it properly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Can we keep going, just ... I'm looking for section 0257. It's page 18.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now in the bottom of this page we are talking about the concept of doctrine, Colonel.

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And 0257, I'll just read it briefly. And if we can go down to the bottom of this page, Mr. Registrar. It is at 0257, [indiscernible] and I will be turning over to the next page: "Doctrine is defined as fundamental principles by which military forces guide their actions in support of objectives. It is authoritative but requires judgement in application. The principle purpose of doctrine therefore is provide alliance armed forces with the framework of guidance for the conduct of operations. It is about how those operations should be directed, mounted, commanded, conducted, sustained and recovered. It is not, therefore, about the past nor is it about the medium or long-term future. It is about today and the immediate future. It is dynamic and constantly reviewed for relevance." Before we -- I ask you a question about this, let me just go down to the next section which is the relationship between policy and doctrine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps for the public to follow it, we could move to page 2-17. When you refer to page 18, it was the page numbering in the e-court system; whereas the page numbering in the document itself starts at 2-16 and we're now at 2-17. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: At 050, and if we just go to the second sentence: "Other factors influence the development of doctrine. It primarily evolves in response to changes in policy, war fighting compatibilities, and/or force employment considerations. Thus it is recognised that policy as agreed by the highest national authorities normally leads and directs doctrine." Now, Colonel, these -- it's your understanding, sir, that NATO comes up with a doctrine on how, generally speaking, NATO is going to operate within the confines of the law of armed conflict, aren't they?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is not only a generic approach because this document, the HVO 1 Charlie, is only the first document of a complete combination of documents that are underlying this document. And the further you go down in that tree of documents, you will find more details and more specific things. This is only the start of it, this is very generic, and this is giving a broad guideline to all the countries that have ratified and implemented this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If I can put this in somewhat graphic terms, if we have the law on armed conflict and this would be a subset, if you will, of the law of armed conflict where NATO, with this doctrine, is trying to deliver how NATO is going to operate, and then you look down, as you noted, to the subsequent items to get more and more specific as time moves on -- as the issue moves on?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this document, Mr. -- Defence counsel, this document exactly does what it describes in what you were reading out before. This document sets out principle purpose of doctrine, generic principles of doctrine inside NATO countries; nothing more nothing less. It gives you the framework for guidance of operations and it does -- it gives commanders in the field how to direct, mount, command, conduct, sustain, and recover operations.
