And that is including everything because later on in the same document, you will find the principles of joined and combined operations, and one of the principles is legitimacy. And there NATO says what they think about legitimacy, and I assure you that inside various NATO working groups where I am a member of, we have huge debate about the application of laws, and I assure you as well that we are not able to solve that completely so every country on its own has its national interpretation on humanitarian law. And especially our debates with representatives of the United States gives us a lot of headaches about how to bring up the international law inside military documentation. And what is being described in this document may be differently described in documents of national states, and I assure you that some words you will not find here, you will find in the Dutch national doctrine; and as I stated before, the Dutch national approach and the Dutch doctrine of my army is, for me, the most important thing, no matter what NATO says about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: You take me to exactly my next point with regard to the difference in doctrine with various countries. We noted previously that the law of armed conflict remains the same. We can have debates about what various things mean, but the law remains the same. But you noted that the Dutch doctrine could be different than US doctrine; and the Dutch doctrine could be different than the Russian doctrine or the Israeli doctrine; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: We see proof of that currently on the television through the Israeli behaviour or the Israeli use of violence against Gaza. That is something that I cannot understand. Maybe that's off the record, but I really cannot understand how you work your way through a civilian-populated area as it is done there; and the Israeli have doctrine, and I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So the answer to the question as we look at various countries, the various countries have different doctrine?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the -- countries are allowed to specify their doctrine to their own needs which means in the alliance that there is an generic basis for doctrine which is this AJP 01, and I assure you that this AJP 01 is ratified and implemented by all countries; but that does not hold countries back. Even if they say we implement this to do it on those things that they want to do. I'm quite sure that every country does it. So doctrine is a generic basis for understanding of operations, but it does not mean that they there will be no difference in doctrine between countries.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I understand, sir?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the Netherlands, the NATO doctrine is practically fully implemented in our national doctrine.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this time, we'd like to offer into evidence 1D65-0172. We will be discussing this further but ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Russo.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: No objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D1247, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D1247 is admitted into evidence. Mr. Konings, may I ask you to make a short break once Mr. Kehoe has formulated his question so as for the transcribers to be able to follow also your answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour, I will try to remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Apparently it's my fault here as well. I've been here a lot long than you have and I still do it. My apologies to the translation booth. And I endeavour together to do our best.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now we have talked about the arms of armed conflict, and we have talked about doctrine and you are familiar with yet another concept, are you not? Known as the rules the engagement, are you not, sir?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: We use in operation rules of engagement, yes, but they differ from operation to operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: That's exactly what we want to get at. Just give me an idea and before we do that, if I can just show you part of your manual which is 1D65-0251. You're familiar with this document, are you not, sir?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am familiar with this document, and I have to say to you, as well, that this document is well, in the process of being rewritten on the movement so there may be differences in what is in this document and what we currently are developing and teaching to our people.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If there is any difference, Colonel, just let us know and the Trial Chamber -- and, of course, we would appreciate it. I would like to turn our attention to this document, and this is a Dutch document that's been translated into English from the Royal Netherlands Army. And I would like to turn to page 4 of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If we can just scroll down a little bit. That's it. Just the rules of engagement, I'm sorry, at the top on section 205.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: It notes that: "The rules of engagement provide guidelines for commanders regarding the nature and the methods for the use of force within the political framework. They are designed to ensure that political authorises can control the use of force within the political and legal framework?" Now, Colonel, you told us before we got into this that rules of engagement change from situation to situation. Can you explain that just in a little bit more detail and maybe you can give us some concrete examples so we can get a handle on it just a little bit better.

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I have to correct you. They are not changing from situation to situation. They are fixed for a complete operation. So we have one set of rules of engagement for the whole operation in Afghanistan, and they go down in exactly, for example, in the permission that you have either to use close air support against a certain target or you have to make a choice for other means or that you even are allowed to attack in certain areas. So they give you exactly building from the basis of doctrine they give you -- and the translation of political guidelines which may even be different from nation to nation. They give you the guidelines that as a commander in the field have you to operate. So you have on all hands, you have your doctrine, all your manuals, and besides that you have laid up on you by your own government the rules of engagement and there is also -- that is done by a national authority. So our own troops in Afghanistan have to make uses of their own rules of engagement, and they are quite often more strict than the rules of engagement built up by a Joint Force Commander; and that can apply the use of violence in certain areas, the way how have you to handle refugees, how you have to handle if you make prisoner of war what you have to do with them, who is responsible for taking care of them, who is transporting them. I gave you the explanation about the collateral damage estimate. Collateral damage estimates as we use them in Afghanistan are part of those rules of engagement. So they give you strict guidelines about, for example, use of weapons systems, whether yes or no in certain circumstances.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So if I can just take what you just said. For instance, in Afghanistan, you have doctrine and then within Afghanistan you have rules of engagement as to how the Dutch armed forces are going to operate.

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, let's take your situation in Afghanistan and would those rules of engagement be different than the deployment of the Dutch army in say SFOR in Bosnia after 1995?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were a different set of rules of engagement because the operation was a different operation. It was in a different circumstances because what is absolutely crucial when you go into an operation and when you set a -- when you build a set of rules of engagement is that you understand the operating environment that you are going into it and with the operating environment, I do not only mean the military context of that. I mean everything. And because we have to realise that the military instrument is just a small portion of what is happening around us. We are a political instrument used by the politicians and we have the unique ability to be able to use violence against other people, against other -- against infrastructure but we are only a part of a whole system what we call the comprehensive approach. And for that reason, each operation that we are involved is different. So for each operation that we are involved, the standard set of doctrine is applicable. So the AJP 01 or the AJP 3 or the AJP 3.2 or the field manual that you showed me from our army is applicable in every operation that we do. But it is -- well, let's say spear pointed, pointed to that operation to make the specific circumstances work, and that is -- was very different rules of engagement in the period after 1995 than what we have in Afghanistan. And you know also that before 1995, UNPROFOR had its own rules of engagement which described exactly what UNPROFOR was allowed to do, yes or no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Konings, the answer to the question therefore is yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour, I tried to keep short.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The only thing that was asked of you whether these rules of engagement in Afghanistan were different from the ones in Bosnia after 1995. If Mr. Kehoe wants to know more, he will not hesitate to ask you the further reasoning behind your answer. But could you please focus primarily what he asks you because your answers tend to be longer and longer, and Mr. Kehoe as he knows is under certain time restrictions.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I will try to keep myself short that's my --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If at the end, you think that you had not had an opportunity to tell us something very important for you, you will have an opportunity to add anything to your previous answers. Please proceed, Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Just one question based on your last answer. The rules of engagement for SFOR after 1995 in Bosnia were much more restrictive, were they not, compared to the rules of engagement for the Dutch army in Afghanistan today; is that not correct?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I cannot give you an answer, yes or no, because then I would need to be capable to compare those to each other because I do think that in certain aspects the rules of engagement in Afghanistan are as restrictive as they were in the SFOR period as well, especially when it concerned our attitude against civilian population.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this time, we'd like to offer into evidence 1D65-0251.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: No objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D1248, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Colonel I would like to show you a manual it is from the United Kingdom Ministry of Defence, the manual of the law on armed conflict. That would be 1D65-0142. If I can just bring that up on the screen, on the first page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we continue, I do not see any translation uploaded. It's in English. That's --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I do believe that is accurate, Mr. President, on the other document. I got these manuals I believe -- I'm not sure if it's this one --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, just to establish that where usually -- of all of the evidence we have two languages available but this is not the case. I do not know what the position of the other Defence teams will be in this respect, and I'm not saying about the one word on the cover page which is still in Dutch even. I hear of no objections, so therefore we leave it for the time being as it is. And I take it that this is a waiver of applying for a translation. The relevant parts have been read to the witness. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Just looking at this particular volume, are you familiar with this, this volume?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let's just talk a little bit about the content.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If we can move to the next page. I believe we have uploaded one page, page 53. And if we could focus on the top of that page, Mr. Registrar. If we can just scroll up a little bit.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And I recognise that this is directed to UK forces. If you take a look at the first sentence: "The law of armed conflict must not be confused with rules of engagement." Down to the next paragraph: "The law of armed conflict derives from, and is part of international law, and is to a large extent universal and settled in its application. Rules of engagement are directives for operational commands and will be subject to constant review within the constraints of the law, according to the political and military assessment of national or multi-national interests as it relates to the mission to be accomplished and the circumstances facing the force. Rules of engagement reflect not only legal consideration but also a wide range of other concerns such as the need to avoid destroying certain installations which is sought to capture intact, to avoid politically damaging criticisms, to harmonise practice among allies and to prevent so-called friendly fire." Colonel - and I realise that are you not a lawyer - is that your general understanding of the relationship between the law on armed conflict and the rules of engagement?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do think that this first part of the publication summarises it a very clear way.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this time, we'll offer 1D65-0142 into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Russo.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm not sure if we have the full document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Is the full document being moved in [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: No, just this page.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: That's fine, Judge, I just want to reserve the opportunity to move in other parts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that becomes Exhibit D1249.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Here, by the way, the same is true as far as translations is concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes. If you can just blow that up just a little bit. Maybe a little less so. Apologies. Okay. That's good. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Colonel, can you see that okay?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: What the Defence has attempted to do here is, based on your experience, is to try to with this graphic demonstrate the permissible ranges of conduct in war, the most expansive, of course, being the laws of armed conflict and then moving to something less expansive which is the military doctrine, be it NATO or country to country. And then what you just referred to as the rules of engagement. Those rules that you use in a specific deployment or operation. Would this accurately reflect your understanding of the relationship between the laws on armed conflict doctrine and the rules of engagement?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'm not quite sure that I understand the relationship through this drawing. It just says to me -- I'm not sure where you're aiming at, at describing a relationship now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If we start from the premise that the outer limits of a less permissible in law is guided by laws of armed conflict, and then a country or an entity such as NATO's individual doctrine is operating within that. And then as you mentioned, when you talked about moving down the chain you then have more rules such as rules of engagement in a particular operation which will operate within doctrine, would this chart not actually reflect that progression from what is allowed most expansively under the law to the individual doctrine of a country and then to the rule of engagement concerning a particular operation.

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in itself not completely, I think, because we already saw before that rules of engagement are not specifically only aiming at -- at lawful aspects. They are aiming at -- they can aim at many other things to arrange certain, certain tricky points in an operation. So yes, of course, there is a connection with -- I'm sorry with the law of armed conflict, and I do see that doctrine is -- is within that law of armed conflict. I fully agree with you there. But I'm not quite sure that I draw the rules the engagement in that way that it's only confined within doctrine. It is also -- it is also outside I think the law of armed conflict. You arrange many national things with that, with the rules of engagement. They may have to do with the law of armed conflict. They may have to do with doctrine, but they may also have to do with other aspects of an operation. So I can imagine -- I can understand why you draw it in this way so ...

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Putting aside the aspects of the rules of engagement that don't apply to the use of the military force that is in a particular location on a particular operation. Just put aside -- I understand that you're talking about something that could be political, something that could be well outside the realm of a military's operations. But within a particular military operations, you would agree with me that the rules of engagement by the Dutch army in Afghanistan operate within Dutch military doctrine, and that military, Dutch military doctrine, is within the law on armed conflict?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the latter I agree with you, that the military doctrine is inside the law on armed conflict. But I'm still not agreeing with what you say about the rules of engagement. Because a military operation is not only a military thing. A military operation consists --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Konings, may I?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Part of the question was, and that's how Mr. Kehoe started: "Putting aside the aspects of the rules of engagement that don't apply to the use of military force." So the question is limited to the rules of engagement, to the extent that they cover the use of military force. Would you then agree that the rules of engagement in that respect should be within --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I agree.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- the boundaries of doctrine and that the boundaries of doctrine would be -- the doctrine would be within the boundaries of the law of armed conflict.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I understand what are you saying, but I still have troubles in phrasing my answer in this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's keep matters simple. For example, if the rules of engagement say help the local population in getting better water supplies and at the same time say don't use any heavier artillery than 120-millimetre. We're talking about the second, only about the second, the use of military force and, of course, there are always shady areas at how to protect and helping the people. But the rules of engagement in relation to the -- could I say the primary, military purpose of that operation should they stay within the limits of doctrine and within the limits of the law on armed conflict.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I exactly now see what you are aiming at, Your Honour, and then my answer would be yes; but I would like to make an comment to that as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Make a brief comment, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My brief comment will be that I understand that for the sake of this question, that we isolate military matters, but unfortunately in practice this is just not possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do understand that. But for this question we have done that, and it is an artificial exercise. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this time, we'd like to offer into evidence 1D65-0256.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: No objection Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D1250, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D1250 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Colonel, if we can just take this down a little bit and going from the various issues, we talked about the law on armed conflict, doctrine, and rules of engagement, I have to thank you for giving some of the manuals that we were provided to by you; and I was interested in looking at some of your entries in your report, and I believe one of the manuals that you used was in 1D65-0001.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Your Honour, this is the face page of the manual that you turned over to the Office of the Prosecutor that was provided to us that you used, is it not sir?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have used this particular document in preparing my first report, knowing that what the title says preliminary study package; but this document is based on the original formal document, which I have gave to the OTP as well and you. That's not translated in English. And this is the official fire support document that we use in the Dutch army and this was a preliminary translation for that, and I used that because it is translated in the proper English for my report because otherwise I had to translate the whole book.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I appreciate that, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm not going to -- I have some excerpts that I'm going to use out of this that I will demonstrate. This is a very large document, and I don't see the need to offer the whole document into evidence. So if counsel would like it as such, I will gladly do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Take us to the pages you would need and then upon deciding whether or not to be admitted we might give an opportunity to Mr. Russo as we did before.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes. Colonel, what I did, if I can put on the screen now 1D65-0385. And this is a red line comparison, Colonel, from the document that we just saw, the field -- the Dutch field manual on brigade fire support as well as your expert report.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If we could go to the next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And what I have done through the course of this, we've done through the course of this is compare the two and examining your deletions and your subtractions. You would agree that the vast majority of the items that were in your -- and this is information that is from your annex A of the first report, you took from the Dutch manual. Is that right, the army field manual?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And in most cases you took it word for word?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry, can you repeat it?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: In most cases you took it word for word from the manual and put it into your report?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Kind of as a cut-and-paste job?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, I'm interested in several places in this where you have added to the manual. And on this document, if we could turn our attention to page 16 and 17. And if ... it would be one more page, please. Now, the -- the bottom half of that is section 8010 [sic] which to a degree of paraphrased and shortened a bit here. I'm interested in the last sentence as it goes over to the next sentence. And it notes: "The artillery assets can only be used --" if we go to the next page. Mr. Misetic corrected me it is 0810 and not 0810 and not 8010. That would be at line 22. Just staying with this: "The artillery assets can only be used in case the save distance between expected impacts and civilian population is big enough to avoid casualties?" Now where in -- I attempted to look through this Dutch field manual, and I looked in vain in the manual as to where this rather categorical statement about use of artillery assets can only be used in case the safe distance between the expected impacts and the civilian population is big enough to avoid casualties. Is that written like that in any place in the manual?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: What do you mean by that? Is your question that you want to have technical details about the safe distance?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: No, sir. My question is that the most of this is a verbatim quote from the manual, and I want to direct your attention to a significant addition which you included in your expert report that being that artillery assets can only be used in case the save distance between the expected impacts and the civilian population is big enough to avoid casualties? That is a categorical statement that is in your expert report, and I want to know where that is in the Dutch field manual or if you have some other manual that supports that rather categorical statement.

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: It may have not been in the translation that I gave to you. But I have to -- to look in the Dutch -- the official version that I have, whether -- where it -- where my statement is coming from. So I cannot give you the proper answer right now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President, maybe we can just to that at the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Konings in the manual of which you -- on which you relied apparently heavily in producing your text, if you could, after the break, inform us where to find the basis in that manual for this statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I would --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: While we're doing that, Colonel, if we could just stay with a couple of other items. If we could just stay on that page, and you say: "Targeting of pure civilian targets will be out of the question since an operation at the tactical level is planned and executed against military targets." If we move down seven lines: "The basic rule will be not to inflict casualties or damage to civilians or property." Now what is the source of that particular issue not to inflict casualty or damage to civilians or property?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is taken from the book that I have here. I'm quite sure I even know the paragraph where it is. I can only read that out in Dutch -- in the Dutch language. I hope that it can be translated and this also comes from the interpretation from what is in this book because the book that I have here, the field manual fire support, is originating, I think, in the year 2000, 2001; and that also is the interpretation made by me after consulting a legal colleague of mine how we treat the eventual attack on civilian population or civilian property. But the basis of what I said here is in this field manual.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this time, we'll offer into evidence 1D65-0385.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Russo.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have no objection to that. Is the additional -- the document which is quoted in there, the 001 also being offered?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Is that the --

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: That is the one that is before, the one that --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] [Overlapping speakers] ... if counsel would like that we'll offer that as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But let's be very practical. That is a very lengthy document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Very.

utterances.text: What I suggest is that you look at that document, see to what extent, apart from the portions selected in this comparative document, to look at what you would need and then to ask that to be added to the evidence. utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: I wasn't demanding that the earlier one be -- and then I just wanted to know if both were being admitted, but if it's just this one, I have no objection to this document on the screen being admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
