utterances.text: Your Honours, that's document ID number 1D65-0385, and it becomes Exhibit D1251.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One second, please. Yes. It is admitted into evidence. Mr. Russo, when would we hear from you if you would like to add to this comparative document.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: If, Your Honour, I could have 'till the end of counsel's examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You mean Mr. Kehoe's examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then there is still half an another day to go, at least Mr. Kehoe. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, Colonel, just looking at these comments, the artillery assets can only be -- only be used in case the safe distance between the expected impacts and the civilian population is big enough to avoid casualties that, sir, is not a reflection of the law on armed conflict, is it?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's yours statement, not mine.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, is it a reflection of the law on armed conflict or is it doctrine according to the Dutch military?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in that case, the only thing can I say about that this is reflected in our doctrine is checked by our legal advisors, and it is their job to compare it with humanitarian law, not mine.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, let me turn your attention to -- and I would ask if this is it an accurate reflection of the training that you received.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If I can bring up 1D65-0148. This is the department of -- the United States army field manual, the law of land warfare. I'm trying to get the quickest page. If we go to e-court page 8 -- 18, excuse me, if we could blow up 25 in the right-hand column. In the paragraph the enemy status of civilians and the last sentence in that 25: "It is generally -- it is a generally recognised rule of international law that civilians must not be made the object of attack directed exclusively against them."

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, based on the training that you've had and your experience, Colonel, that is the outer limits of the law on armed conflict, i.e. that civilians cannot be made the object of attack; is that right?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what it says, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: That is very different from a situation such as you have reflected where you note that artillery assets can only be used in case the safe distance between the expected impacts and the civilian population is being enough to avoid casualties. That is a very different concept --

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's a different concept, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, just for my information I see that the cover page says 1956, and then on the second page, I find 15th of July, 1976 and since you showed quite a keen interest in the development, I wondered whether this to be understood the publication of 1976 and whether there are any updates on this document, since then.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Your Honour, there are numerous updates, and the updates are constant. They keep -- the page itself remains the same but what happens in the department of defence - I'm not sure if it's true in the countries - but in the United States, you get a notice that these three pages have been removed, and serve these three pages. But the volume itself of the law of warfare remains static, but they just update it continuously. That is my best explanation based on my experience.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now how to know the portion you read dates from what year between 1956 and 2009.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: This particular document, the front page on this is, I believe, 1956. I think this is a old, well-established aspect that has not changed. That particular provision. Other provisions within that volume have. But this particular is still as the Colonel just mentioned the state of the law, i.e., that obviously civilians cannot be the object of attack.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There is at least a prohibition against an attack on civilians, it's what the outline of that exactly is and to what extent it includes customary law whether it is based on conventions that were ratified by the United States is not clear to me yet, but I just say this so you know what questions would remain on my mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If we can with move, Colonel, to another section on this volume, and if I may. If we could move to page 5 of this document. And it is under the rubric of unnecessary killing and devastation. And it talking about the prior paragraph if I may, talking about the -- hitting military objectives. "Particularly in the circumstances referred to in the preceding paragraph, loss of life and damage to property incidental to attacks must not be excessive in relation to the concrete and direct military advantage expected to be gained." Now looking at these items in conjunction with your report, it is clear, to you, not, Colonel, that the laws on armed conflict prohibits the purposeful infliction of casualties on civilians; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: So far I'm with you, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: It does not -- the law on armed conflict, does not prohibit knowing non-purposeful infliction of civilian casualties, does it?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I cannot say yes or no. You only showed me a US document from 1956 which I have not been able to study. So to me, that doesn't say anything so far. And if I may be able to one remark about some of the formal paragraphs it only talks about warfare between two states which is something different in -- in the international world than what is quite obvious happens around us. That's the reason that from the Dutch perspective we have been improving our view on how to outside weapon systems yes or no. And again I have not been able to read this before. I only see a small portions of that. It is only a US document with the vision of the United States, and there is as I told you before, quite some difference in opinion between the legal approach of an operation from the Dutch perspective or the US perspective.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Then let's go back to what you in fact wrote in your report, and I go back to your report in P1259, your first report if we can turn to page 2 subsection g, little x. Do you have that, sir, your report or we can bring it up on the screen --

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can take it myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: -- just take it might be easier for you.

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which -- can you recall the paragraph?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Sure, on the first report, it's 1259; second page it's g, subdivision 10, Roman numeral X, which looks like an X, but it is Roman numeral, 10.

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Midway through this paragraph, you note, that: "These indirect effects," and you're talking about artillery: "These indirect effects may be unintended in case military targets close to a civilian area have been attacked?" So you realise do you not, Colonel, that in the use of artillery against a military target that is not purposefully directed against the civilian population there is an consideration that it may result in civilian casualties and that as long as those casualties are damage or not excessive [Realtime transcript read in error, "successful"] in relation to the military advantage gained that type of artillery attack is permissible under the law on armed conflict. Isn't it?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again I have only seen a United States document which refers to the law on armed conflict. I haven't seen that law. And with that in mind, it is very important what you said yourself is that it should not be excessive and for that reason our explanation of that is - and I specifically want to state, our, Netherlands explanation of that is - that we avoid using artillery in case we expect any damage or casualties on the civilian side. Especially when the value of that military target is so low that it is not interesting to attack that target or if attack by artillery is not useful because you cannot do anything to the target with artillery. I cannot look to those -- to the things that we are discussing without every time, over and over again, take all the aspects into account that are important. And it is our translation from our own manual that we give commanders the -- the -- the direction, Don't use artillery when you have this chance on civilian casualties.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Russo.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Just to correct a portion of the translation at page 67, line 17 the word successful I believe Mr. Kehoe intended and actually said damage which is not excessive in relation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I think that's right. Thank you sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's what I heard as well. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: In your report you are categorical about using the use of artillery when in fact, sir, it's an issue of proportionality, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's an issue of proportionality, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: What is proportionality? And if I can refer you to your report, you refer to proportionality in the list of factors to take into consideration on page 5 of your report and 6 of your report, 6 b and in number 7 the application of the proportionality principle? What is that, sir?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Proportionality to my opinion is that once you attack a certain target with -- with whichever military mean that have you available that the value of that target should be, as such, that the use of violence is permitted, and that the damage done is kept to an absolutely -- to the lowest minimum that you can get.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And in a situation where there are military targets in a civilian area the question that a commander has to ask himself or herself is whether the -- with this target possibly in a civilian area will there be a loss of life and damage to the property that is not excessive in relation to the military advantage gained. That is the weighting system he does. Isn't it?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have never denied about that. I agree with you about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: When we apply the proportionality principle and a commander makes a decision to fire into a civilian area, the decision is not per se illegal even if there is collateral damage. It only becomes problematic if the damage to the civilian population is excessive in relation to the military advantage gained; right?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, to my -- my recollection when do you that, it is becoming illegal; when the damage is excessive it becomes illegal.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Exactly. If the damage is excessive in relation to the military advantage gained?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And that is a decision that a military commander has to make based on a wide variety of circumstances in a combat arena, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not deny that. That's absolutely true because that's -- yes that is absolutely true. But also to that, the decision made by the commander has to be led also by the rules of engagement that are applicable for that operation. So he is never free in doing what he likes. He is the one that takes the decision, but it is his responsibility, and it's a large responsibility; and I understand how difficult that is for commanders on the scene that he has to apply also those rules of engagement. And those rules of engagement may very well have in it and certain the fact that you have to take care, that you have to use your violence in such a way that do you in the apply harm to civilian property at all, which is the background of the collateral damage estimate of 500 metres in Afghanistan.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And that's a rule -- and that rule of engagement that you just described is a rule of engagement that is within the laws of armed conflict and is more narrow than what is permissible under the laws of armed conflict; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think you may -- that's the right conclusion.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I don't know if you want to take a break right now. But I'm about to move to another subject. But before we do this, if I could tender 1D65-0148.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would just ask for the same amount of time to choose additional portions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So there's no objection against admission, but you may come with a request to add something.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours that becomes Exhibit D1252.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D1252 is admitted into evidence. We'll have a break, and we'll resume at 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Colonel, did you have a chance at the break to find out in your manual where the manual has the sentence: "Artillery assets can only be used in case the safe distance between the expected impacts and the civilian population is big enough to avoid casualties." Did you find that in the manual?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: This specific sentence is not in the manual.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let us turn back to your report, if we may, and I'd like to turn to -- and this is P1259, page 6, and this is paragraph 6 b, ii, right under the application of proportionality. I think we have to go -- four pages up. Yeah, that's it. Now, Colonel, after you've -- according to your recitation of the factors an ending with the application of the proportionality principle you then talk about selection of the assets.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If we can just go up a little further. Keep going. Two little i there. Right there. Actually there is a -- okay there we go. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, you note in your report at ii that once these and other aspects have been considered the best available asset for the attack will be designated. Now let us focus on the best available asset. You would agree, Colonel, based that upon a country's resources the best available asset might be different. In other words the best available asset for the United States might be different than the best available asset for -- in this case Croatia, or for some other country, say, who's fighting right now. Maybe for even the Israelis. The best asset might be different; right?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And as technology evolves that best available asset changes too; right?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not always.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Sometimes it does?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: It may become more sophisticated, hopefully?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: When a reasonable commander is making a decision about the best available asset, that reasonable commander has to make a practical decision based on assets he has at his disposal; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Okay. Now, let us continue --

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wanted to -- sorry to interrupt -- I want to --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And, Colonel, please, any time you want to elaborate on something and explain, please do. I don't want to cut of off, ever.

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: You are fully right. He is dependent on the assets that he has available for that action, but he also has available the decision not to use assets at all; and then we come back to the proportionality and the excessive damage and the value of a target; so I would like to make that very clear that a very good decision can be not use violence at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Absolutely. And again this is the asset you have, the proportionality issue --

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: -- whether or not damage is going to be excessive and return to the actual military advantage?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: One moment, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Excuse me, Colonel.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If I may, Your Honour, I have just been made aware of something by Mr. Misetic on page 71 line 11: "Did you find that in the manual?" And the answer is, "This specific sentence is not in the manual," but it looks like the question. Maybe that can be cleaned up at a later date, but I just bring it to the Court's attention.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I do agree that the question was, "did you find that in the manual?" And the answer was this specific sentence is not in the manual. This kind of errors may be caused by not making breaks. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If I may, I would just like to go back to the comparison of the field manual that's in your report. That's in D1251. And I'd like to -- and this is again looking at your annex a to your report, and looking at page 49 in D1251, under the assessment -- under the title of "Damage assessment." This is the area that you took from the manual at paragraph 0252 and according to the report, you have added this that I have underlined in purple over to the right. And in talking about damage assessment: "It may be clear that the assessment of a physical attack with lethal munitions may be easier in comparison with the situation when non-lethal weapons/means have been used. Battle damage assessment therefore deals with looking to the effects that have been achieved and the control whether the achieved effects are indeed the intended ones. Actions may have the intended effects, but commanders have to take into account the fact that every action always will have unintended, long-term effects as well." Now, that particular item, sir, is not in the manual, and frankly I don't know what you're talking about there. What are we talking about there? You're talk being psychological effects? I mean what are you referring to there, sir?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is one of the effects that I'm referring to. But not only effects to damage done to infrastructure. Every other affect that occurs when you use lethal weapon systems, or when you use lethal weapon systems with the intention to bring non-lethal effects and then I just play it out clear using artillery in order to frighten people. That's the way that you have to think about assessment of attacking or using weapon system or military means, at all, inside an operation; and the reason that that is no in the military field manual is just the fact that it will be in the new manuals that we are currently writing because there it will take the larger portion of how we describe an operation. And since have I been asked by the OTP to describe fire support, the use of fire support, I didn't limit myself in purely repeating what was in the field manual; but I have introduced, I have in certain as well, some developments. And the discussion around effects and you may be familiar with the term of effects based approach to operations which is a US, the US started that, and is going far beyond the effects that are caused, the physical effects that are directly visible after a physical attack, and that's what I tried to explain here in a very few sentences, knowing that the debate around effects, and the effects of actions in an operation, and unintended effects, long-term effects -- I can name you -- there are much more effects -- that is -- that is -- the crucial thing in our new doctrinal -- doctrinal documents, not only in the Netherlands but also in other armies and in NATO because - and I know that this is a lengthy statement, Mr. -- Your Honour - but I have to say that because thinking about the facts is crucial for our -- the way we conduct our operations, and the way we build up our operations. And the very difficult part are the so-called non-lethal effects and non-lethal occur in a population. They are psychological they have to deal with infrastructure, they can be visible after years. They -- that's the point I try to make here, so it is not in the original document. That is absolutely true, but it's a development that we take into account now. You may have heard from the term information operations which is something that's the most important thing in our operations currently; and that says already the use of non-lethal means to try to complete your operation and get away from the use of lethal means. And I try to reflect that -- this in my report in order to give an idea that there is more than only artillery.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And I appreciate that, Colonel, the reason I focus on this is that this is your description of what is and what is going to be published as the current Dutch doctrine. Isn't it?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not only the current Dutch doctrine but it's the same development in international doctrine.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: But it is not a reflection of the laws on armed conflict; it is doctrine, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is doctrine.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, continuing on in your report and we're locking at the effective fire. And if I can turn to the next page in the document on the screen, 1D1251, page 50. Now, just going through the -- some of the items and I know I will go through this quickly because you did refer to it at least obliquely during the course of your testimony on direct. And when you were talking about the various reasons why artillery would be used -- and one of the things that you took a limited view on is the use of artillery for the destruction of actual buildings; is that right, sir?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And let me put on the screen 65 ter 5879, which is a -- another United States department of army excerpt. This is fire support in land battle. And I think if we go to page 24 in this document. And if we can blow up the centre and the destruction aspect of this. I just want to develop the destruction issuing, Colonel, in the context of Operation Storm, if we could, taking some of the comments in your report and also some of your testimony yesterday. And in this, it notes: "In attack system that destruction puts a target out of action permanently. Direct hits with high explosive or concrete piercing shells are required to destroy hard materiel targets. Usually, destruction requires large expenditure of ammunition and is not considered economical." Colonel, you agree that is consist with your view of destroying buildings in the former Yugoslavia, is that right? Excuse me, in Knin?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now if we talk about destruction in the context of Operation Storm, we have a different situation in that you knew, Colonel, that the HV was trying to liberate the Krajina and bring that area or bring it back into the Republic of Croatia; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Okay. So there would be, during this artillery attack, no reason to try to level Knin or destroy these buildings if the Republic of Croatia intended to use these buildings again and was just trying to incorporate this land in to the Republic of Croatia, right?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this time, I'll offer into evidence 65 ter 5879.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar -- I'm sorry, Mr. Russo, I should have said.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I'm just saying yes, Judge.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that becomes Exhibit D1253.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D1253 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If we can flip back to D1251 and go to the bottom of page 52 where we talk about interdiction fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Colonel, I'm not going through every aspect of it because much of your report follows the manual verbatim. I'm trying to focus on areas where you added something or there seems to be a change; and one of them is on the interdiction category.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If we can go to page 52 in this document. Is that page 52? There it is. It's on there now. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: "Interdiction fire delivered at a point target or an area within the aim of preventing the enemy using that abject area, scattered mines" -- excuse me, scattered mines are -- I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: You got to turn the page, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let me read that again: "Interdiction fire fired delivered at a point target or area within the aim of -- with the aim of preventing the enemy using that object or area. Scatterable mines are one means of achieving this." Now, just talking about interdiction fire by itself. There is nothing in and of itself in violation of the laws of armed conflict by using interdiction fire, is there, i.e., firing into an area to prevent the enemy from using that area?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: In so far, no. I have not stated that in my -- everywhere in my document that interdiction fire should not be used.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I want to go to the next sentence that you added on: "Quite useful when aimed against the civilian area, one can recall during the Balkan conflict the illegal attack on water collection points and market places." Now that, sir, is not in the manual and is based solely on your experience in Sarajevo, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: The situation in Sarajevo that you experienced, was a situation that was much different than what was transpiring during Operation Storm on the 4th and 5th of August of 1995, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: I'd like to object to the question, generally being vague, if the question could be more specific about what was different.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I would agree, Judge. That was a terrible question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, well then make a better one.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: General [sic], what you were investigating or what you worked on in Sarajevo was the firing on a -- I don't know wanted to say daily, basis but almost daily basis by the Serbs into Sarajevo onto civilian targets with an army never coming in with an attempt to engulf Sarajevo and take it over; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So that was much different than what we had in Operation Storm where we had an artillery attack that was then followed by an effort by the HV at some point difficult in the Dinara, but an effort by the HV to retake this land to make it part of the Republic of Croatia; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: You don't mind that I do not agree completely with you because it is too easy for me to come to that conclusion that you make. And there might be a similarity in the situation although Knin was not surrounded for three and a half year, Knin was to be liberated by the HV army, and nothing can be said -- the use of -- of this type of fire is very well possible in every scheme of manoeuvre that can you think about. So the comparison between the two cities in itself, you're right, it's different, total different situation; but it doesn't prevent the fact that you cannot use artillery in civilian-populated areas in a situation like in Knin. And you were talking about the HV entering the city after an artillery attack. Well, I haven't seen that because there was some sort of artillery attack on the city of which I do not know what the effects were that the Croatian army wanted to achieve because the effects are nowhere stated at least not in the information that have I. So I have no clue what effect they wanted to have. And the actual seize of the city, Knin, occurred lots of hours after the initial attack, and I have already explained that seeing the combination of an artillery attack 36 hours later, the enter of the city by the Croatian brigade, Croatian troops, the absolute, to my opinion, low value of the military targets, the military targets inside the city, I cannot then understand what is then the military connection between that artillery attack and the actual entering of the city. Seeing the low value of those military targets, as a military commander, I would have spared my artillery to use for -- in case I needed it really.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Colonel, I appreciate that can you only operate based on information that you were given, but we will get to more information that apparently was not given to you. Do you agree or disagree that the artillery attack on Knin was done in conjunction with an ongoing offensive by the HV against the ARSK?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the very wide -- in the very wide operational framework you can say that the -- that the artillery -- in the information that I was reading, the artillery attack was connected to the overall Operation Storm. I don't say anything with this statement about the way it was actually executed because then we have to go back to the operational order, and I still do not have any information about what was meant by shelling the town of Knin. No effect, nothing whatsoever and that brings me absolutely to the conclusion that I have written here in my report.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And we will get do that, Colonel, with more information I want to stay with your report. We will get there in due time. And I want to move to the next aspect of your report which is harassing fire. The manual says that -- and this is it on the same page on the screen, page 353: "Harassing fire is fire intended to cause confusion among the enemy, to curtail movement, and by threatening lossers [sic] to lower morale." Now, the use of artillery fire as harassing fire to curtail this conduct of the enemy is a legitimate lawful purpose of artillery or the use of artillery, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I haven't said that it isn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Given that it is subject to the rule of proportionality, right?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Again this type of -- you write, you add on: "This type of fire is also extremely useful impermissible use against civilian areas. When used, it causes physical losses but more important, it influences complete civilian societies in a very disturbing and negative way. I refer here to my personal experience as an UNMO leader during the seeming of Sarajevo." Now, again you are comparing this to harassing fire in Sarajevo or writing this, your commentary, you discussing harassing fire in Sarajevo that is not in done [sic] with part of an ongoing military operation to take the Krajina; right?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I think we said that -- okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, I think you said, "I think we said that --" I don't know whether that was extension of your question, but you were -- the translators couldn't follow your speed of speech.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, under the circumstances and the information you were given, harassing fire going into Knin can be used against the military to cause confusion, suppress their movement, and lower their morale; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: You think it only becomes improper when it is directed against the civilian population; right?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And in the context when a commander is making a decision to fire into military targets to suppress that activity, once again his decision on harassment has to be balanced by the rule of proportionality; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Okay. But if his intention by that conduct is to impede the enemy from moving, re-supplying, and operating, and causing confusion as well as lowering morale, that is a legitimate purpose of artillery, of course, subject to the rule of proportionality; correct?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not deny that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, let us turn to your report in this --

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: May I ask you a question on this, because --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Konings, if you want to say something in addition to your answer that's fine, but we are usually not reversing the one who asks questions and the ones who answers questions; but if you want to make an additional -- if you want to add anything to your answer, then ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm doubting, Your Honour, I probably will repeat myself when saying this, because I think the way the questions are asked is only focussing on the military purpose of these fires. But I have already said before that, so far, I haven't seen any explanation in the information given to me what the effect would be when an operational commander gives the order to his troops to shell a complete city because that is it my crucial point. That is my crucial point because that is my experience and that is a -- I throw it in the open that is my -- my true conclusion when you read something in an operational order, like shelling the city of Knin, that has made me write down as I have written down the stuff that have I written down here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I do agree with you that it is to some extent repetitious what you now say. We are carefully listening to your answers and we try not to forget your previous answers when you give a new answer. Don't worry about the focus of Mr. Kehoe because Mr. Kehoe performs his duty in this courtroom as Defence counsel.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay. I fully understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Colonel, let us turn to the emission of artillery that you talk about in the red line; it's on page 56. We talk about the emission of artillery and you make a general statement about the emission of artillery: "Field artillery, destruction, neutralisation, or suppression of the enemy using indirect fire from a gun and/or missile system as an integrated element of the fire, report system synchronised with the combined operations, operations of manoeuvre units." And we'll get into the synchronised operations, Colonel, and we have a lot more information to discuss with you that apparently was not discussed by the OTP. But I'm interested in the next sentence that you added: "In recent years, this mission has added more elements such as the use of lethal means to achieve non-lethal effects, but in relation to this expert report artillery asset have [sic] been used to support military operations that in fact were aimed against civilian targets." Now were you told --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, your quote was not correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I'm sorry, I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May have been used, that is not the same as having used. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: "May have been used to support military operations that in fact were aimed against civilian targets." Now, Colonel were you told by the Office of the Prosecutor that the HV in Operation Storm used military assets in support of a military operation that were purposefully aimed against the civilian population. Were you told that?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: What you are talking about here is what, based on your experience in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I'm talking about here is a general statement, this statement has nothing to do with Knin with the operation that we're talking about now. It's just a statement that in the repeat years the mission of artillery units has changed because artillery used in -- also in a non-lethal way, in warning, in harassment, and whatever we have discussed before; and I have stated that that has happened in the past to support military operations and which part of that military operation was apparently aimed against civilian targets, and that is not only referring to my experience in Sarajevo which is part of that statement, of course, I cannot deny that. I have been there, it was six -- seven months of my life. It made a great impression on me, and it is also coming from the fact that in current military operations weapon systems, not only artillery, are in various cases used against civilian targets, and I quote what I said before. We see it every day on the TV.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, Colonel, taking the evidence that you were provided by the Office of the Prosecutor, and let's be very frank about this statement. Looking at the evidence you were provided by the Office of the Prosecutor did they give you any piece of information any document that demonstrated that artillery was aimed at civilian targets in support of a military operation? Anything. And if they did, what is it?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: They gave me -- the information they gave me, in that -- no, I have to start that over again. In the information they gave me, the first thing - and I will be frank as well - the first thing that struck me the most was reading the sentence shelling the city of Knin without any explanation at all. Because -- well, I have explained that numerous times before why that struck me. That is not given to me by the OTP and the conclusions I made are my own conclusions. And further we have worked along the lines of the documents that you have been presented as well and especially concentrating on the lines on the lists shown to me of the targets available inside Knin of which we debated whether they were military targets or non-military targets or low valuable targets as we did in the past days. So the -- the biggest point in my report and which causes those blue lines as well is the sentence that I already said before.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So this is your opinion. It is not based on any document, specific document or piece of information that you received during the course of your examination?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is based on what I read in the documents that were given to me by the OTP, and I was asked by the OTP to comment on that and I based and I wrote the report, and I based the addendum on that. I'm sorry I only can repeat that --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I understand that --

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Unless there is a good explanation a very good explanation for the sentence shelling the city of Knin then I will stick to my statements that I have made before. Because that -- okay, I'll leave it at that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Colonel, trust me, we're going to get plenty of opportunity to either re-evaluate your position. I would like to turn our attention to the actual logic and formulation of a plan to attack Knin under the circumstances and let's just something that is pretty basic and -- and if we can turn our attention to D1248, which is the combat operations, Dutch combat operations manual that we talked about before, the one you said was being updated and we're looking for page ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We have to wait for a second until the transcriber was able to re-boot.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It has been fixed. Thank you very much for the efforts by everyone to fix the system. Mr. Kehoe, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Turning to this -- this document back to the combat operations manual for the Royal Dutch Army, and if we look at page 4 and just briefly like to talk to you about military targets as described in -- no. Is it there? Yes it is. Second paragraph, in the second paragraph, the second full sentence, Colonel. It notes that: "Military targets are those objects which, because of their nature, location, designation or use contribute actively to the operation -- military operation, excuse me, and of which the complete or partial destruction, capture, or rendering inoperative in the prevailing circumstances would produce a clear military advantage." Now, Colonel, I understand that is a rather straightforward definition of military targets. It is it only problematic when those targets are in centres of civilian or in and around areas where civilians are as we have been talking about. And in this particular case when you were going through it, the decision to put those military targets in civilian areas was a decision made by the ARSK, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: When we take that into consideration, and we're not going to through the proportionality issue as to -- the idea of excessive damage in relation to the concrete military advantage, one thing you talked about previously was -- and I believe this is in direct examination, was the issue of the possibility of a frontal assault or a movement of the troops by -- of the HV into Knin, and Mr. Russo showed you, I believe, the document that showed 1900 members of the 4th Guards Brigade. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, when a commander is and using the rule of proportionality and he is making a decision, weighing the importance of the military objective against possible damage to civilian property or individuals, what is not part of that equation is the idea that he has to -- to accept increased risk for his troops. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: We don't look to that in the way you describe it, because the commander should take that into account. Let me put it very, very clear. Opposite to each other, if you can save lives of civilians, and it will take lives of your own soldiers, you might have to take that decision. That's what your commanders are teached [sic]. Nothing less, nothing more.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: But that's Dutch doctrine, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's Dutch doctrine. And I told you before that my basic origin and my basic -- the basics on which I based my expert report is coming from Dutch doctrine. I'm in the armed forces for 35 years.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And I appreciate that, sir. And I appreciate that. But we're dealing with the law on armed conflict, and I want to be clear with you that in gauging the rule of proportionality, a reasonable commander does not have to factor in increased risks to his troops, does he? That's not part of the equation under the law of armed conflict.

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that. But I don't think that is written there, that a commander has to take more own casualties in order to provide civilian casualties. I don't think it is written there in such a way, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm about to move into a rather large topic at this point. I don't know, given the circumstances --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If it takes far more than five minutes, then -- if you don't have a small one, then --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I don't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- perhaps we better adjourn for the day. Mr. Konings, I would like to give you the same instruction as I gave you before; that is, not to speak with anyone about your testimony, whether given already or still to be given, and we'd like to see you back tomorrow, 9.00 in the morning, in this same courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: May I ask you a question, a very short question, Your Honour? I don't want to waste your time, but from the discussion around the table, I hear that you may need me next week as well. I would appreciate to have a certain time schedule in order to arrange it at home and at my work.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I do understand. I should have raised the issue, as a matter of fact, and not leave it until tomorrow . From what we heard from the parties until now, there is a fair expectation that your testimony could be concluded next Tuesday. But I'm not giving any guarantees. It might be Wednesday morning as well. If this would cause you major problems, then --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I don't think we have Wednesday court.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: There is no court on Wednesday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Oh, there is no court on Wednesday. But we have a long Tuesday, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: We have a long Friday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We have a long Friday. Then it will not be Wednesday but it might be Thursday then, if we cannot conclude on Tuesday. If that would cause you any problems, please tell me so that we can see what we can do about it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I understand that I will be hear tomorrow, the whole day, so we have two sessions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We start tomorrow in the morning, but we have no afternoon session.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That means that we will finish at approximately a quarter to 2.00.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay. That -- otherwise, it would have caused some problem. Not now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And the Monday and the Tuesday --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Is no problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No problem. Thursday morning. We try to avoid that, but ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It should be a problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Should be no problem. Thank you very much for your cooperative attitude. We adjourn, and we'll resume tomorrow, Friday, the 16th of January, 9.00 in the morning, in Courtroom I.
